title: DN-QSM: Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping via Laplacian Field Estimation and Regularized Null-Space Correction

synopsis.Motivation: Background-field contamination and ill-conditioned dipole inversion limit quantitative susceptibility mapping.
synopsis.Goal(s): Adapt Deep Null Networks for QSM through learned field estimation, analytic inversion, and regularized spectral correction.
synopsis.Approach: Two 3D U-Nets were trained using AHEAD-derived simulations and evaluated on COSMOS and in vivo brain hemorrhage MRI.
synopsis.Results: COSMOS normalized root-mean-square error decreased from 44.38% to 37.36%, a 15.8% relative reduction. Supplied iQSM and pretrained NeXtQSM yielded 48.97% and 76.96%. In vivo evaluation was qualitative.

impact: DN-QSM adapts Deep Null Networks to susceptibility mapping using AHEAD-derived simulations. Its analytic initialization and learned spectral correction reduced COSMOS reconstruction error. In vivo brain hemorrhage imaging demonstrates application to clinical acquisitions, motivating independent quantitative validation.

body.INTRODUCTION: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) estimates tissue susceptibility from magnetic-field perturbations. Background-field contamination complicates local-field recovery, while zeros of the dipole kernel make susceptibility inversion ill-conditioned.[1] Learned approaches, including NeXtQSM[2] and iQSM,[3] address reconstruction through data-driven mappings. We introduce DN-QSM, which builds on Deep Null Networks[4] and separates Laplacian-guided local-field estimation, Tikhonov-regularized inversion, and learned spectral correction. The central design is to weight the correction toward frequencies attenuated by the regularized inverse. We evaluate this formulation using a COSMOS-based simulation and in vivo brain hemorrhage MRI.
body.METHODS:
The architecture comprises two separately parameterized 3D U-Nets (Figure 1). The masked total field is mean-centered and extended outside the brain mask before a Fourier-domain discrete Laplacian is applied. This extension avoids differentiating an abrupt mask truncation. The first network estimates the local field, using root-mean-square (RMS) normalization of the Laplacian input and a normalized-field skip connection. Both networks use residual instance normalization to retain an amplitude-dependent feature pathway.

Let $D$ denote the dipole kernel, $\mathcal{F}$ the Fourier transform, and $\hat b_{\mathrm{loc}}$ the estimated local field. The initial susceptibility is $\chi_0=\mathcal{F}^{-1}[K_\tau\mathcal{F}(\hat b_{\mathrm{loc}})]$, with $K_\tau=D/(D^2+\tau^2)$ and $\tau=0.1$. The second network receives RMS-normalized $\chi_0$ and predicts a residual, rescaled to susceptibility units as $r_\phi$. The final reconstruction is $\hat\chi=\chi_0+\mathcal{F}^{-1}[P_\tau\mathcal{F}(r_\phi)]$, where $P_\tau=1-DK_\tau=\tau^2/(D^2+\tau^2)$. The regularized null projection is a smooth spectral weighting that emphasizes frequencies with small $|D|$.

Training data were simulated from 105 original susceptibility maps from the Amsterdam Ultra-high field adult lifespan database (AHEAD),[5] partitioned into 95 training and 10 validation samples. Simulations included exterior-source background fields, noise, susceptibility lesions, and localized dephasing. Joint supervision combined local-field, field-gradient, exterior-field, initial-susceptibility, final-susceptibility, and dipole-consistency losses. The final joint fine-tuning run comprised 30 epochs from pretrained weights using AdamW, batch size 8, and initial learning rate $3\times10^{-5}$. Epoch 18 was selected by minimum COSMOS normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE).

The quantitative experiment used one fixed COSMOS-based simulation with a $160^3$ reference grid, 1-mm isotropic spacing, simulated background fields, and SNR 100. Comparisons included the Tikhonov initialization, official pretrained NeXtQSM, and a supplied iQSM reconstruction. NRMSE was computed over the full three-dimensional brain mask without fitted intensity scaling, offset correction, or mean removal.

In vivo evaluation used one brain hemorrhage MRI dataset acquired on a 3T Siemens Trio with a 12-channel head coil and six-echo gradient-echo imaging: first TE/echo spacing, 4.92/4.92 ms; TR, 35 ms; flip angle, $15^\circ$; voxel size, $0.8\times0.8\times2.0$ mm; acquisition time, 4 min 51 s. Supplied unwrapped phase underwent magnitude-squared-weighted echo-time fitting, conversion to ppm, and resampling to 1-mm isotropic resolution. DN-QSM used $184^3$ and $201^3$ inference grids for COSMOS and in vivo data; NeXtQSM used $192^3$ and $256^3$. Outputs were cropped to common brain regions. In vivo assessment was qualitative because reference susceptibility was unavailable.
body.RESULTS: COSMOS NRMSE was 44.38% for the Tikhonov initialization and 37.36% for final DN-QSM, corresponding to a reduction of 7.02 percentage points (15.8% relative). Supplied iQSM and pretrained NeXtQSM yielded 48.97% and 76.96%, respectively. Figure 2 presents reconstructions and signed reference differences under identical display limits. In vivo reconstructions (Figure 3) exhibited differences in tissue and vascular contrast across methods. Residual streaking remained visible near strong susceptibility sources; the available data do not support a quantitative accuracy ranking for the in vivo case.
body.DISCUSSION: The COSMOS experiment supports the proposed combination of analytic initialization and frequency-weighted learned correction. Its explicit additive decomposition identifies the contribution beyond regularized inversion. However, the experiment does not isolate the effects of Laplacian preprocessing, normalization, or spectral weighting. COSMOS also guided checkpoint selection, making the reported error a development result. Only one simulation and one in vivo dataset were evaluated; independence of the training samples and COSMOS reference remains unverified. Method-specific padding and unavailable iQSM inference settings further limit comparator interpretation. Independent datasets, controlled preprocessing, and component ablations are required to assess generalization and attribute performance gains.
body.CONCLUSION: Based on Deep Null Networks, DN-QSM combines Laplacian-guided field estimation with Tikhonov inversion and regularized null correction. It reduced COSMOS development-case NRMSE by 15.8% relative to initialization and produced in vivo brain hemorrhage susceptibility maps, motivating independent quantitative validation.

figures.name: Architecture
figures.caption: DN-QSM, based on Deep Null Networks. A boundary-aware Laplacian precedes local-field estimation by a 3D U-Net. A Tikhonov regularized inverse provides initial susceptibility. A second 3D U-Net predicts a residual; regularized null projection weights this residual before addition to the initial estimate. Blue: learned modules; gold: fixed operators.

figures.name: COSMOS
figures.caption: COSMOS comparison: susceptibility reconstructions (top) and signed reference differences (bottom). Columns: NeXtQSM, iQSM, Tikhonov regularized inverse, final DN-QSM, and reference. Titles report whole-mask 3D NRMSE. Grayscale limits are +/-0.1 ppm for susceptibility and +/-0.02 ppm for differences. COSMOS also guided checkpoint selection.

figures.name: In vivo
figures.caption: In vivo brain hemorrhage reconstructions acquired at 3T. Columns: NeXtQSM, supplied iQSM reconstruction, Tikhonov regularized inverse, and final DN-QSM. Each column shows matched central axial, sagittal, and coronal views. Grayscale limits: +/-0.1 ppm. Reference susceptibility was unavailable; evaluation is qualitative.

author_notes: Add authors, affiliations, presenting-author information, funding, and final data-use acknowledgements in the submission portal. These are not part of the blinded abstract body.

The authors identify AHEAD as the source of the 105 susceptibility maps. Record the AHEAD version, source-map identifiers, and preprocessing; verify subject-level splitting and separation from the COSMOS reference.

The authors identify the in vivo image as a brain hemorrhage acquisition on a 3T Siemens Trio with a 12-channel coil, six-echo GRE, first TE and echo spacing 4.92 ms, TR 35 ms, flip angle 15 degrees, 0.8 by 0.8 by 2 mm voxels, and acquisition time 4 min 51 s. One dataset is evaluated here; no cohort size is inferred from the acquisition description. Add the relevant ethics/consent and clinical data-use information.
Verify the earlier checkpoint's complete training history. The 30 epochs describe the final fine-tuning run; the selected checkpoint is from epoch 18.
Confirm that the supplied iQSM files correspond to the intended COSMOS and in vivo inputs, and document version, settings, and output units.
COSMOS was used for checkpoint selection, so the reported NRMSE is a development-case result. Training/reference independence should be documented before claims of independent test-set performance.

Method-specific padding is preserved: DN-QSM uses 184-cubed/201-cubed grids, and NeXtQSM uses 192-cubed/256-cubed grids for COSMOS/in vivo. Padding affects DN-QSM outputs and should be controlled in future comparisons.

DN-QSM is based on the Deep Null Networks formulation and uses a regularized spectral weighting. This smooth weighting does not impose the exact null-space constraint or inherit exact data-consistency guarantees of an orthogonal null-space projection.

Figure labels use Tikhonov regularized inverse for the analytic initialization. Next-QSM headings refer to official NeXtQSM. The in vivo figure uses the updated iQSM2 file recorded in provenance. Reference 5 uses a shortened article title.
